How to learn frontend (and keep improving) · 7/7

Detect, then branch

  1. 1Test the feature
  2. 2True: enhanced code
  3. 3False: fallback code

Your code asks one question: can this browser do it?

The answer picks the enhanced code or the fallback code.

The screen shows three feature tests.

The @supports rule tests CSS inside CSS.

CSS.supports runs the same test in JavaScript.

The in operator checks an object member.

CSS.supports asks the browser about grid-template-columns subgrid.

True: the page links subgrid-layout.css.

False: the link does not change, and the default layout stays.

The in operator asks if navigator has a geolocation member.

If yes, the page uses the Geolocation API.

If no, the else branch offers static maps.

Some features cannot be tested, so you may load a polyfill.

Its code runs on your page.

In 2024, the polyfill.io domain was sold, and its script

was changed to inject malware into more than 100,000 sites.

An origin trial lets your site use an experimental feature.

You register, get a token, and add the token to your page.

When the trial expires, the feature is gone, so keep the fallback.

Test the feature, run the enhanced path when it exists,

and keep a working fallback when it does not.
